mcqs.question: What specifically breaks in the Bird/Penguin hierarchy shown on this slide?
options: Sparrow and Eagle can no longer be instantiated once Penguin is added
Penguin's override of fly() has to violate the contract every other Bird honors, by throwing instead of flying
Java doesn't allow a subclass to override a method that has a body in the parent
The compiler rejects the code because Penguin doesn't implement fly() at all
mcqs.explanation: The hierarchy assumed every Bird can fly(); Penguin can't, so its override has to lie by throwing instead. Existing subclasses are unaffected, Java allows overriding methods with bodies, and the code compiles fine — the problem is behavioral, not syntactic.

mcqs.question: Per the compare table, when does composition clearly win over inheritance?
options: When the relationship is a stable is-a with no variant likely to violate it
When you want the simplest possible constructor with zero collaborators
When a new variant might violate the parent's contract, or two independent axes of variation need to combine
Whenever performance is the primary concern, since composition is always faster at runtime
mcqs.explanation: Composition earns its cost when a subtype might not honor the parent's full contract, or when independent behaviors need to combine without a subclass explosion. A stable is-a relationship favors inheritance instead, and composition isn't inherently faster — it adds a layer of indirection.

mcqs.question: What's the actual signal that composition has gone too far, per this follow-up?
options: Having more than three behavior objects in any single class
Needing a builder, factory, or DI container just to assemble one object correctly, because the collaborators are too tangled to wire up simply
Any use of an interface as a constructor parameter
The class no longer being unit-testable in isolation
mcqs.explanation: There's no fixed collaborator count — the tell is when assembling the object needs its own supporting machinery because the parts are tangled. An interface parameter or a moderate object count alone isn't the problem, and well-composed classes are usually more testable, not less.

mcqs.question: A candidate answers "never use inheritance, only composition" as an absolute rule. What's the issue?
options: It overcorrects — a stable is-a relationship, like a small closed set of shapes sharing one real invariant, is still a legitimate use of inheritance
It's actually correct, since composition strictly dominates inheritance in every case
Inheritance is required by definition in every object-oriented language, so banning it is impossible
Composition can only be used with interfaces, never with abstract classes, so the rule is technically meaningless
mcqs.explanation: The rule of thumb is a guideline, not a ban — a genuinely stable is-a relationship is still a clean fit for inheritance. Composition doesn't strictly dominate (it has real indirection cost), and neither of the other claims about language mechanics are true.
